text: The Boeing F/A-18E and F/A-18F Super Hornet are a series of American supersonic, twin-engine, carrier-capable, multirole fighter aircraft derived from the McDonnell Douglas F/A-18 Hornet. The Super Hornet is in service with the United States, Australia, and Kuwait. The F/A-18E is a single-seat variant and the F/A-18F is a tandem-seat variant, both of which are larger and more advanced versions of the F/A-18C and D Hornet, respectively. Capable of air-to-air and air-to-ground/surface missions, the Super Hornet features an internal 20 mm M61A2 rotary cannon and can carry air-to-air missiles, air-to-surface missiles, and other weapons. It can carry up to five external fuel tanks for additional fuel and can be configured as an airborne tanker with an external air-to-air refueling system. Designed and initially produced by McDonnell Douglas, the Super Hornet first flew on 29 November 1995. Low-rate production began in March 1997 and reached full-rate production in September 1997, following the merger of McDonnell Douglas and Boeing the previous month. An electronic warfare variant, the EA-18G Growler, was also developed. Although officially named "Super Hornet," it is commonly referred to as "Rhino" within the United States Navy. The Super Hornet entered fleet service with the U.S. Navy in 1999, supplanting the Grumman F-14 Tomcat, which was retired in 2006; it has served alongside the original Hornet as well. The F/A-18E/F became the backbone of U.S. carrier aviation since the 2000s and has been used extensively in combat operations in the Middle East, including the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, and against the Islamic State and Assad-aligned forces in Syria. The Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF), which operated the F/A-18A as its main fighter since 1984, ordered the F/A-18F in 2007 to replace its aging General Dynamics F-111C fleet, with the RAAF Super Hornets entering service in December 2010. The Super Hornet is planned to be replaced by the F/A-XX in U.S. Navy service starting in the 2030s. The Super Hornet is an enlarged redesign of the McDonnell Douglas F/A-18 Hornet, with its wing and tail configuration tracing its origin to a Northrop prototype, the P-530, circa 1965, which was a rework of the lightweight Northrop F-5E with a larger wing, twin tail fins, and a distinctive leading edge root extension (LERX). Later flying as the Northrop YF-17 "Cobra," it competed in the U.S. Air Force's Lightweight Fighter (LWF) program, losing to the YF-16, but the Navy found the twin-engine YF-17 design more suitable for carrier operations and selected it over the navalized YF-16 derivative. After selecting the YF-17, the Navy directed that it be redesigned into the larger F/A-18 Hornet to meet a requirement for a multi-role fighter (VFAX) to complement the larger and more expensive Grumman F-14 Tomcat. Northrop teamed with McDonnell Douglas to navalize the design, with McDonnell Douglas becoming the prime contractor. The Hornet proved effective but limited in combat radius. The concept of an enlarged Hornet was first proposed in the 1980s and marketed as "Hornet 2000," an advanced F/A-18 with a larger wing and longer fuselage to carry more fuel and more powerful engines. The end of the Cold War led to military budget cuts and restructuring. The McDonnell Douglas A-12 Avenger II Advanced Tactical Aircraft (ATA) was canceled in 1991 after serious problems; it was intended to replace the obsolete Grumman A-6 Intruder. The Navy then embarked on the Advanced-Attack (A-X) program but also considered updating an existing design as an interim capability until A-X could be fielded. McDonnell Douglas proposed the "Super Hornet" (initially "Hornet II" and later "Hornet 2000" in the 1980s), which could serve as an alternate replacement for the A-6 Intruder or an interim aircraft for A-X; the design would also address limitations of the previous F/A-18 models, such as insufficient bringback capability. The next-generation Hornet design proved more attractive than Grumman's Quick Strike upgrade to the F-14 Tomcat, which was regarded as insufficient and opposed by Secretary of Defense Dick Cheney. The A-X, which evolved into the A/F-X due to added fighter capabilities, was canceled in 1993 during the Bottom-Up Review as the Super Hornet was viewed as a more attractive low-risk approach due to post-Cold War budget reductions. The Grumman F-14 Tomcat was the Navy's primary air superiority fighter and fleet defense interceptor. Cheney described the F-14 as 1960s technology and drastically cut F-14D procurement in 1989, canceling production in 1991 in favor of the updated F/A-18E/F. The decision to replace the Tomcat with an all-Hornet Carrier Air Wing was controversial; Vietnam War ace and Congressman Duke Cunningham criticized the Super Hornet as an unproven design that compromised air superiority. Between 1991 and 1992, the Navy canceled the Navy Advanced Tactical Fighter (NATF), a navalized variant of the Lockheed Martin F-22 Raptor, due to escalating costs. As a cheaper alternative to NATF, Grumman proposed substantial improvements to the F-14 beyond Quick Strike, but Congress rejected them as too costly and reaffirmed its commitment to the less expensive F/A-18E/F. Originally viewed as an interim for A-X or A/F-X, the Super Hornet became the mainstay of the Carrier Air Wing. The Super Hornet was first ordered by the U.S. Navy in 1992, with the total Engineering and Manufacturing Development (EMD) cost capped at $4.88 billion in FY 1990 dollars (~$10.3 billion in 2024). The Navy retained the F/A-18 designation to sell the program to Congress as a low-risk "derivative," though the Super Hornet is largely a new aircraft. The design of the F/A-18E/F was driven by a cautious development approach favoring incremental improvements over the F/A-18C/D, affordability, and reliability at the expense of raw performance. The Hornet and Super Hornet share many characteristics, including avionics, ejection seats, radar, armament, mission computer software, and maintenance/operating procedures. The Super Hornet's F414 engines are derived from the Hornet's F404 and incorporate advances developed for the A-12's F412. The initial F/A-18E/F retained most of the avionics systems from the F/A-18C/D configuration to reduce upfront development costs. The design has an empty weight slightly greater than the F-15C. Manufacturing division mirrors the Hornet's, with McDonnell Douglas (later Boeing) responsible for the forward fuselage, wings, and stabilators, while Northrop Grumman produced the center/aft fuselage and vertical tails. The design service life was 6,000 flight hours. The Super Hornet first flew on 29 November 1995. Initial production began in 1995. Flight testing started in 1996, with the first carrier landing in 1997. Low-rate production began in March 1997 and full production began in September 1997. Testing continued through 1999, finishing with sea trials, aerial refueling demonstrations, and design modifications to resolve "wing drop" and possible stores release interference. Testing involved 3,100 test flights covering 4,600 flight hours. The Super Hornet underwent U.S. Navy operational tests and evaluations in 1999 and was approved in February 2000. Following the retirement of the F-14 in 2006, all of the Navy's combat jets were Hornet variants until the F-35C Lightning II entered service. The F/A-18E and F/A-18F took the place of the F-14 Tomcat, A-6 Intruder, Lockheed S-3 Viking, and KA-6D aircraft. The EA-18G Growler replaced the EA-6B Prowler. The Navy refers to this reduction in aircraft types as a "neck-down." During the Vietnam War era, the Super Hornet's roles were performed by a combination of the A-1/A-4/A-7 (light attack), A-6 (medium attack), F-8/F-4 (fighter), RA-5C (recon), KA-3/KA-6 (tanker), and EA-6 (electronic warfare). It was anticipated that $1 billion in fleetwide annual savings would result from replacing other types with the Super Hornet. The Navy considers the Super Hornet's acquisition a success, meeting cost, schedule, and weight (400 lb, 181 kg) below requirement threshold limits. The total Super Hornet procurement number fluctuated significantly during production. The 1997 Department of Defense (DoD) Quadrennial Defense Review cut the originally planned number of around 1,000 by nearly half. By October 2008, Boeing had delivered 367 Super Hornets to the U.S. Navy, but the service was still experiencing a strike fighter shortfall as older aircraft retired and procurement was insufficient, especially with ongoing combat operations in Iraq and Afghanistan and delays in the F-35 program. In 2006, the Navy was 60 fighters below its validated requirement. The FY2010 budget bill authorized a multiyear purchase agreement for additional Super Hornets, finalized on 28 September 2010, that reportedly saved $600 million over individual yearly contracts. This contract for 66 Super Hornets and 58 Growlers was intended to mitigate a four-year delay in the F-35 program. In 2019, Boeing received a $4 billion contract to deliver 78 Block III Super Hornets for the Navy through fiscal 2021. The Navy plans to sign year-to-year contracts to convert all of its Block II aircraft to Block III variants through 2033. As the F-35 began entering service, Boeing announced plans to end Super Hornet production in 2025, later extended to 2027 with an additional 17 orders from the U.S. Navy. The Block II Super Hornet incorporates an improved active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar, larger displays, the joint helmet mounted cueing system, and several other avionics replacements. Avionics and weapons systems under development for the prospective production version of the Boeing X-32 were used on the Block II Super Hornet. New-build aircraft received the APG-79 AESA radar beginning in 2005. In January 2008, it was announced that 135 earlier production aircraft were to be retrofitted with AESA radars. In 2008, Boeing discussed the development of a Super Hornet Block III with the U.S. and Australian military, featuring additional stealth capabilities and extended range. The airframe is strengthened to increase service life to 10,000 flight hours, and some Block II aircraft can be modified to achieve this. In 2010, Boeing offered prospective Super Hornet customers the "International Roadmap," which included conformal fuel tanks (CFT), enhanced engines, an enclosed weapons pod (EWP), a next-generation cockpit, a new missile warning system, and an internal infrared search and track (IRST) system; the IRST was later mounted on the centerline external tank. The EWP has four internal stations for munitions, a single aircraft can carry a total of three EWPs, housing up to 12 AMRAAMs and 2 Sidewinders. The next-generation cockpit features a 19 x 11-inch touch-sensitive display. In 2007, Boeing stated that a passive Infrared Search and Track (IRST) sensor would be a future option, mounted in a modified centerline fuel tank, detecting long wave IR emissions to spot and track targets such as aircraft; combat using the IRST and AIM-9X Sidewinder missiles is immune to radar jamming. In May 2009, Lockheed Martin was selected by Boeing for the IRST's technology development phase, with a contract following in November 2011. As of September 2013, a basic IRST would be fielded in 2016 and a longer-range Block II version in 2019. The sensor would be designated the AN/ASG-34(V) IRST21. An F/A-18F performed a flight equipped with the IRST system in February 2014, and Milestone C approval authorizing low-rate initial production (LRIP) was granted in December 2014. Sequestration cuts in 2013 caused years of delay, and the Navy chose to skip the basic version and transition directly to the Block II IRST for operational service. After initial production quality issues, the IRST became operational in January 2025. Boeing and Northrop Grumman self-funded a prototype of the Advanced Super Hornet, featuring a 50% reduction in frontal radar cross-section (RCS), conformal fuel tanks (CFT), and an enclosed weapons pod. Features could also be integrated onto the EA-18G Growler: using CFTs on the EA-18G fleet was speculated as useful for relieving underwing space and lowering the drag margin for the Next Generation Jammer. Flight tests of the Advanced Super Hornet began on 5 August 2013 and continued for three weeks, testing the performance of CFTs, the enclosed weapons pod (EWP), and signature enhancements. The U.S. Navy was reportedly pleased with the flight test results and hopes it will provide future procurement options. Although the Advanced Super Hornet was not pursued, many elements would be transferred to the Block III. In 2013, the U.S. Navy was considering the widespread adoption of CFTs, which would allow the Super Hornet to carry 3,500 lb (1,600 kg) of additional fuel. Budgetary pressures from the F-35C Lightning II and Pacific region operations were cited as reasons supporting the use of CFTs. Flight testing demonstrated CFTs could slightly reduce drag while expanding the combat range by 260 nautical miles (300 mi; 480 km). The prototype CFT weighed 1,500 lb (680 kg), while production CFTs are expected to weigh 870 lb (390 kg). Boeing stated that the CFTs do not add any cruise drag but acknowledged a negative impact on transonic acceleration due to increased wave drag. General Electric's enhanced performance engine (EPE), increasing the F414-GE-400's power output by 20%, was suggested as a mitigating measure. In 2021, the U.S. Navy halted plans to fit CFTs as standard on all Block III Super Hornets due to cost, schedule, and performance issues. In 2009, development commenced on several engine improvements, including greater resistance to foreign object damage, reduced fuel burn rate, and potentially increased thrust of up to 20%. In 2014, Boeing revealed a Super Hornet hybrid concept, equipped with the EA-18G Growler's electronic signal detection capabilities to allow for targets engagement using the receiver; the concept did not include the ALQ-99 jamming pod. Growth capabilities could include the addition of a long-range infrared search and track sensor and new air-to-air tracking modes. The Super Hornet is largely a new aircraft at about 20% larger, 7,000 lb (3,200 kg) heavier empty weight, and 15,000 lb (6,800 kg) heavier.

The Super Hornet is a significantly larger aircraft than the original Hornet, weighing about 7,000 lb (3,200 kg) more in empty weight and 15,000 lb (6,800 kg) more in maximum weight, with an empty weight approximately 11,000 lb (5,000 kg) less than the F-14 Tomcat it replaced, though it does not match the F-14’s payload or range. It carries 33% more internal fuel, increasing mission range by 41% and endurance by 50% over the Legacy Hornet. The aircraft features a 34-inch (86 cm) stretched fuselage and a 25% increased wing area, yet has 42% fewer structural parts than the original Hornet. The wings include a dogtooth extension and a porous strip at the folding joint to mitigate "wing drop." The General Electric F414 engine, derived from the F404, provides 35% more thrust over most of the flight envelope and is rated at 22,000 lbf (98 kN) in afterburner, with a proposed 20% increase in power output via a F414-GE-400 variant suggested as a mitigating measure. The Super Hornet can return to an aircraft carrier with over 9,000 lb (4,100 kg) of unspent fuel and munitions, known as "bringback." It has larger rectangular caret inlets with fixed ramps for the more powerful engines and two additional wing hard points (for a total of 11), retaining previous hardpoints on the bottom centerline, wingtips, and two conformal fuselage positions. Enlarged leading edge extensions improve vortex lifting in high angle of attack maneuvers and reduce static stability margin, resulting in pitch rates exceeding 40 degrees per second and high resistance to departure from controlled flight. All underwing pylons are slightly canted outward due to early wind tunnel testing concerns, though this was later deemed unnecessary, and production tooling was adjusted to retain the canted pylons to save development costs. The Super Hornet employs a balanced approach to survivability, incorporating reduced radar cross-section (RCS) through design features such as inlet alignment to scatter radar waves, fixed fanlike reflecting structures to divert energy, panel joint serration, edge alignment, and elimination of unnecessary surface gaps and resonant cavities; its frontal RCS is an order of magnitude smaller than prior generation fighters, and additional RCS reductions can be installed as needed. The F/A-18E/F has 90% avionics and software commonality with the F/A-18C/D fleet initially, with upgrades introduced in successive Blocks. It features a quadruplex digital fly-by-wire system, a digital flight-control system that detects and corrects battle damage, and initially uses the APG-73 radar, later replaced by the AN/APG-79 AESA radar, which enables simultaneous air-to-air and air-to-ground attacks, higher-resolution ground mapping, detection of smaller targets like inbound missiles, and tracking of air targets beyond the range of air-to-air missiles. The first AESA-equipped Super Hornets were certified for independent flight and maintenance by VFA-213 on 27 October 2006. The Joint Helmet Mounted Cueing System (JHMCS) was first delivered to VFA-213 on 18 May 2007, providing multi-purpose situational awareness including high-off-boresight missile cuing. The Shared Reconnaissance Pod (SHARP) offers high-resolution, digital tactical reconnaissance with day/night and all-weather capability. The MIDS-JTRS communication system upgrades the Multifunctional Information Distribution System, increasing bandwidth tenfold and enabling compatibility with Joint Tactical Radio System standards. Block III aircraft, first delivered in 2021, feature an improved cockpit with all MFDs replaced by a large-area 10 in × 19 in (25 cm × 48 cm) touchscreen display, updated integration and targeting networks, an updated processor, and an open mission systems architecture; Block II aircraft can be upgraded to Block III. The aircraft can carry the AN/ASG-34(V)1 IRST21 sensor in a modified centerline FPU-13 tank, reducing its capacity to 340 gallons, and the ATFLIR is planned to be replaced by the AN/AAQ-28(V) Litening targeting pod. The Super Hornet entered fleet service with the U.S. Navy in 1999 and achieved initial operating capability in September 2001 with VFA-115 at Naval Air Station Lemoore, California, which was also the first unit to deploy F/A-18s into combat. On 6 November 2002, two F/A-18Es conducted a "Response Option" strike in support of Operation Southern Watch, dropping 2,000 lb (910 kg) JDAM bombs in combat for the first time. During Operation Iraqi Freedom, VFA-14, VFA-41, and VFA-115 flew close air support, strike, escort, SEAD, and aerial refueling missions; VFA-14 primarily served as aerial refuelers and VFA-41 as Forward Air Controllers. On 6 April 2005, VFA-154 and VFA-147 dropped two 500-pound (230 kg) laser-guided bombs on an insurgent location east of Baghdad. On 8 September 2006, VFA-211 expended GBU-12 and GBU-38 bombs against Taliban fighters and fortifications west and northwest of Kandahar, marking the first active combat use of the Super Hornet by that unit. During the 2006–2007 cruise with the Dwight D. Eisenhower, VFA-103 and VFA-143 supported operations in Iraq, Enduring Freedom, and off the Somali coast, dropping 140 precision-guided weapons and conducting nearly 70 strafing runs. The Super Hornet can operate from the French aircraft carrier Charles de Gaulle. On 7 August 2014, U.S. defense officials authorized bombing missions against Islamic State (IS) forces in northern Iraq to protect U.S. personnel in Irbil and ensure safety of transport aircraft making airdrops to Yazidi civilians; two Super Hornets dropped 500 lb laser-guided bombs on a mobile artillery piece and later struck a convoy and a mortar position. On 18 June 2017, a U.S. Navy F/A-18E shot down a Syrian Air Force Su-22 fighter-bomber near Tabqa, the first aerial kill of a crewed aircraft by an American fighter since 1999, the first by the Navy since the 1991 Persian Gulf War, the first by a Super Hornet, and the third kill by an F/A-18; the encounter lasted eight minutes and involved an AIM-9X miss followed by an AIM-120 hit. In 2018, Boeing was awarded a contract to convert nine single-seat F/A-18E Super Hornets and two F/A-18F two-seaters for Blue Angels use, to be completed by 2021. On 26 December 2023, Super Hornets from USS Dwight D. Eisenhower and USS Laboon destroyed 12 attack drones, three anti-ship missiles, and two ground attack cruise missiles fired by Houthi forces in the southern Red Sea. On 12 January 2024, U.S. Navy, USAF, and RAF forces struck Houthi targets in response to attacks on commercial shipping in the Red Sea, with Super Hornets from Dwight D. Eisenhower participating in strikes that hit 60 targets at 16 locations using over 100 precision-guided munitions. On 22 December 2024, an F/A-18F from VFA-11 was shot down by USS Gettysburg in a friendly fire incident; both crew members survived. On 28 April 2025, while under attack by missiles and drones from the Houthis, Harry S. Truman made a hard turn and a F/A-18E from VFA-136, being towed in the hangar, fell overboard and was lost at sea. On 6 May 2025, a second Super Hornet was lost when arresting gear failed to catch the aircraft during landing. In 2007, the Australian Government signed a $2.9 billion contract to acquire 24 F/A-18Fs as an interim replacement for the Royal Australian Air Force’s aging F-111s, with the total cost including training and support over 10 years expected to be A$6 billion (US$4.6 billion). The order was controversial, with Air Vice Marshal (retired) Peter Criss stating he was "absolutely astounded" that $6 billion would be spent on an interim aircraft, citing the U.S. Senate Armed Services Committee’s assertion that the Block I Super Hornet’s "excess power" was inferior to that of the MiG-29 and Su-30, both operated or on order by Southeast Asian air forces. Another former senior RAAF officer, Air Commodore (ret.) Ted Bush, also expressed concerns.

Four F/A-18Fs were ordered by the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) as an interim replacement for its aging F-111s, with the order also intended to address potential difficulties in quickly replacing the RAAF's existing F/A-18A/B Hornets in the event of delays to the F-35 program. The total cost of the purchase, including training and support over 10 years, was expected to be A$6 billion (US$4.6 billion). The order was controversial; Air Vice Marshal (retired) Peter Criss expressed astonishment at the $6 billion expenditure on an interim aircraft and cited the US Senate Armed Services Committee, stating that the "excess power" of the Block I Super Hornet was inferior to that of the MiG-29 and Su-30, both operated or on order by air forces in Southeast Asia. Air Commodore (ret.) Ted Bushell stated that the F/A-18F could not perform the strategic deterrent/strike role of the F-111C and that the latter could continue operating until at least 2020. On 31 December 2007, the new Australian Labor government announced a review of the RAAF's aircraft procurement plans due to suitability concerns, lack of a proper review process, and the belief that an interim fighter was not needed. On 17 March 2008, the government announced it would acquire 24 F/A-18Fs; Defence Minister Joel Fitzgibbon called the Super Hornet an "excellent aircraft" and cited costs and logistical factors, noting that the F-111's retirement was "irreversible" and that only the F/A-18F could meet the timeframe, with termination involving "significant financial penalties and create understandable tensions between the contract partners." The Block II aircraft include installed engines and six spares, APG-79 AESA radars, Link 16 connectivity, LAU-127 guided missile launchers, AN/ALE-55 fiber optic towed decoys, and other equipment. On 27 February 2009, Fitzgibbon announced that 12 of the 24 F/A-18Fs would be wired on the production line for future conversion to Boeing EA-18G Growlers at an additional cost of A$35 million, with the final decision on the EA-18G conversion at a cost of A$300 million to be made in 2012. The first RAAF F/A-18F made its first flight from Boeing's factory in St. Louis, Missouri, on 21 July 2009. RAAF crews began training in the U.S. in 2009. The first five F/A-18Fs arrived at RAAF Base Amberley in Queensland on 26 March 2010, followed by six more on 7 July 2010, and four more arrived in December 2010, after which the first RAAF F/A-18F squadron was declared operational on 9 December 2010. In 2008, U.S. export approval was sought for EA-18G Growlers. In December 2012, Australia sought cost information on acquiring an additional 24 F/A-18Fs to avoid a capability gap due to F-35 delays. In February 2013, the U.S. Defense Security Cooperation Agency notified Congress of a possible Foreign Military Sale to Australia for up to 12 F/A-18E/Fs and 12 EA-18Gs with associated equipment, training, and logistical support. In May 2013, Australia announced the order of 12 new EA-18Gs instead of converting any F/A-18Fs. In June 2014, Boeing received a contract for 12 EA-18Gs; the first was rolled out on 29 July 2015. On 24 September 2014, eight RAAF F/A-18Fs, along with a KC-30A tanker, an early warning aircraft, and 400 personnel arrived in the United Arab Emirates to participate in operations against Islamic State (IS) militants. On 5 October 2014, the RAAF officially began combat missions over Iraq using a pair of F/A-18Fs armed with GPS-guided bombs, returning safely to base without attacking targets. On 8 October 2014, an RAAF F/A-18F conducted its first attack, dropping two bombs on an ISIL facility in northern Iraq. In 2017, EA-18Gs replaced No. 6 Squadron RAAF's F/A-18Fs, which were then transferred to No. 1 Squadron RAAF. On 8 December 2020, F/A-18F A44-223 rolled into a ditch while attempting to take off at RAAF Base Amberley, with the crew ejecting; an eyewitness reported smoke from one engine. A day later, the RAAF grounded its fleet of 24 Super Hornets and 11 Growlers while investigating the incident, which was determined to be pilot error. The Super Hornet was repaired and returned to service in mid-2021. In May 2015, the Kuwait Air Force was reportedly planning to order 28 F/A-18E/Fs with options for an additional 12, but in June 2015, it was reported that Kuwait was considering a split purchase between the Eurofighter Typhoon and the F/A-18E/F. On 11 September 2015, Kuwait signed an agreement for 28 Eurofighters. In November 2016, a proposed Kuwaiti sale of 32 F/A-18E and 8 F/A-18F fighters, armaments, and associated equipment was approved by the U.S. State Department. In June 2018, the Kuwaiti Government ordered 22 F/A-18Es and 6 F/A-18Fs via a US$1.5 billion contract, scheduled for delivery by January 2021, but rescheduled due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Boeing has pitched the F/A-18E/F to numerous countries, particularly those operating the legacy Hornet, as a "logical progression from the Hornet to the Super Hornet," with shared logistics, weaponry, and training. So far, only the US Navy, Australia, and Kuwait have ordered and received the Super Hornet. In 2002, Boeing offered Malaysia Super Hornets as part of a buy-back package for its existing Hornets, but the procurement was halted in 2007 after the government chose the Sukhoi Su-30MKM; Chief Gen. Datuk Nik Ismail Nik Mohamaed of the RMAF stated that the air force had not planned to end the Super Hornet buy, noting such fighters were needed. Separately, the Super Hornet is a contender for the MRCA program, under which the RMAF seeks to equip three squadrons with 36 to 40 new fighters with an estimated budget of RM6 billion to RM8 billion (US$1.84 billion to US$2.46 billion), with competitors including the Eurofighter Typhoon, Dassault Rafale, and Saab JAS 39 Gripen. On 12 March 2014, Belgian newspaper De Morgen reported that Boeing was in talks with the Belgian Ministry of Defence about the Super Hornet as a candidate to replace Belgium's aging F-16 fleet. In April 2017, Boeing announced it would not compete in the competition, citing it "does not see an opportunity to compete on a truly level playing field." On 25 October 2018, Belgium officially selected the offer for 34 F-35As to replace its fleet of around 54 F-16s. Boeing proposed the Super Hornet to the Brazilian government in response to an initial requirement for 36 aircraft, with a potential total purchase of 120. In October 2008, the Super Hornet was reportedly selected as one of three finalists in Brazil's fighter competition. However, news of National Security Agency spying on Brazilian leaders caused animosity between Brazil and the US. Brazil eventually dropped the Super Hornet from its final list and selected the Saab JAS 39 Gripen in December 2013. The Super Hornet was a contender to replace the CF-18 Hornet, a version of the F/A-18A and B models operated by the Royal Canadian Air Force. Like the older Hornet, the Super Hornet's design is well-suited to Northern Canada's rugged forward operational airfields, while its extended range removes its predecessor's main deficiency, with commonalities enabling a straightforward transition. In 2010, Canada decided on a sole source selection of the F-35A. Boeing claimed that Canada had ignored the Super Hornet's radar cross-section characteristics during evaluation. By April 2012, Canada was reportedly reviewing its F-35 procurement. In September 2013, Boeing provided Canada with data on its Advanced Super Hornet, suggesting that 65 aircraft would cost $1.7 billion less than an F-35 fleet. The US Navy buys Super Hornets for $52 million per aircraft, while the advanced model costs $6–$10 million more per aircraft, depending on options selected. The Liberal government elected in 2015 indicated it would launch a competition to replace the CF-18 fleet. During the election, Liberal Leader Justin Trudeau stated that his government would not buy the F-35. On 22 November 2016, the government announced its intention to acquire 18 Super Hornets on an interim basis. In September 2017, the U.S. State Department granted Canada permission to buy 10 F/A-18Es and 8 F/A-18Fs (or EA-18Gs) along with supporting equipment, spares, and armaments; the agreed cost totaled CA$1.5 billion, or about CA$83.3 million per aircraft, with the addition of supporting equipment, training, spares, and weapons increasing the acquisition cost to CA$6.3 billion. However, Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau warned that the pending Super Hornet sale, along with a possible sale of another 70, was adversely affected by Boeing's actions against Bombardier Aerospace, such as a complaint to the US government over the sale of CSeries airliners to Delta Air Lines at unduly low prices; in September 2017, the U.S. Department of Commerce proposed a 219% tariff on CSeries imported into the US. In January 2018, the USITC commissioners unanimously ruled against Boeing, stating that the U.S. industry is not threatened and no duties will be imposed. In late 2017, the Canadian government agreed with Australia to purchase 18 used F/A-18 Hornets as an interim measure. Boeing confirmed its bid for the Advanced Fighter Program, likely offering a mix of 88 F/A-18E/F Advanced Super Hornets (Block III) and Boeing EA-18G Growlers. On 25 November 2021, Reuters reported that Boeing is out of the competition since its fighter proposal does not meet requirements, with the F-35 and Saab JAS 39 Gripen remaining in competition. In 2008, the Royal Danish Air Force was offered the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet as one of three fighters in a Danish competition to replace 48 F-16AM/BMs. The other contenders were the F-35A Joint Strike Fighter and the Eurofighter Typhoon. Denmark is a level-3 partner in the JSF program. The final selection was originally planned for mid-2015, with 24 to 30 fighters expected. In April 2014, the Danish Ministry of Defence handed over a Request for Binding Information (RBI) that specifically listed the F/A-18F two-seat variant. In December 2015, the decision was postponed to 2016, with final order details pending negotiations. In May 2016, the Danish government recommended to parliament that 27 F-35As should be procured instead of 38 Super Hornets. In September 2016, Boeing indicated it would take legal action against the Danish F-35A buy, claiming flawed data was used. In March 2018, Boeing lost the case, with the court stating that the authorities' decisions on refusal of access to documents were legal and valid. In June 2015, a working group set up by the Finnish MoD proposed starting the HX Fighter Program to replace the Finnish Air Force's current fleet of F/A-18C/D Hornets, which will reach the end of their service life by the end of the 2020s. The group recognized five potential types: Boeing F/A-18E/F Advanced Super Hornet, Dassault Rafale, Eurofighter Typhoon, Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II, and Saab JAS 39 Gripen. In May 2016, the DOD announced that Boeing (with the Super Hornet) and Lockheed Martin (with the F-35) would respond to the information request. This request was sent in early 2016 with five responses received in November 2016. A call for tender will be sent in spring 2018 and the buying decision is scheduled to take place in 2021. The F/A-18IN Super Hornet, equipped with Raytheon's APG-79 AESA radar, was considered by the Indian Air Force (IAF) in August 2008 when Boeing submitted an industrial participation proposal involving partnerships with Indian companies. The IAF conducted extensive evaluations, including field trials in August 2009, but eliminated the F/A-18IN from the competition in April 2011, selecting instead the Dassault Rafale. In October 2016, India received three unsolicited bids, including one from Boeing for the Super Hornet, to replace its MiG-21 and MiG-27 fleets. The Super Hornet is now competing with six other aircraft in the MMRCA 2.0 tender for 114 multi-role combat aircraft. On 17 January 2017, the Indian Navy issued a Request for Information (RFI) to procure 57 fighters under the Multi-Role Carrier Borne Fighter (MRCBF) programme for INS Vikrant, requiring day-night and all-weather operations, shipborne air defence, air-to-surface and buddy-buddy refuelling, reconnaissance, and electronic warfare, with deliveries spanning three to six months after contract signing. By June 2017, Dassault (Rafale M), Boeing (F/A-18E/F), Saab (Gripen Maritime), and UAC (MiG-29K) had formally responded. Talks with Dassault and Boeing began by 2018, with a Strategic Partnership (SP) model expected that year, and the Navy finalising its Naval Air Staff Requirements (NASR). By December 2020, the MRCBF fighter number was reduced to 36 due to a proposal by DRDO and ADA to develop the HAL TEDBF indigenously, with plans to merge the MRCBF procurement with the IAF's MRFA. In the same month, Boeing, in coordination with the U.S. Navy, demonstrated the F/A-18’s STOBAR capability at Naval Air Station Patuxent River through eight ski-jumps. On 6 January 2022, a 12-day Rafale M demonstration took place at the 283-metre-long shore-based test facility at INS Hansa, with the deal to be in Government-to-Government (G2G) mode and the quantity reduced to 26. Between 20 May and 15 June 2022, two F/A-18E/F Block III completed operational demonstration tests at the same facility, including multiple ski-jumps, roll-ins, and fly-in-arrestments in various configurations, confirming compliance with Indian Navy carrier requirements. By 7 December 2022, the Indian Navy headquarters reported that the Rafale was the front runner after meeting all criteria. On 13 July 2023, the Defence Acquisition Council (DAC) granted Acceptance of Necessity (AoN) for 26 Rafale M F4 for the Indian Navy and three additional Kalvari-class submarines. Negotiations began on 30 May 2024 with Navy, Defense Acquisition Wing, Dassault, and Thales. By late June 2024, the base price of the Rafale was set equal to that of the IAF. On 3 September 2024, the DAC dropped integration of the Uttam AESA radar and indigenous weapons like Astra missiles due to high costs and an estimated 8-year delay. By 29 September 2024, Dassault submitted its final price offer for 26 aircraft. The squadron will be based at INS Dega, Visakhapatnam, forming the Carrier Air Group of Vikrant. The deal, valued at over ₹63,000 crore (US$7.5 billion), includes Meteor (air-to-air), Exocet (anti-ship), SCALP (cruise) missiles, five-year performance-based logistics support, and training for crew and equipment, including Indian Navy-specific design alterations such as helmet-mounted display, low band frequency jammers, improved radio altimeter, VHF range decoys, and software changes for air-to-sea mode, EMI, and EMC. By 3 February 2025, price negotiations were completed. The Cabinet Committee on Security cleared the deal on 9 April 2025. The IN-specific Rafale Ms will be showcased within 18 months and all aircraft delivered within 37 to 65 months after contract signing. The deal was signed on 28 April 2025, comprising 22 single-seat carrier-compatible aircraft and four twin-seat aircraft used solely from land bases, with the first four delivered by 2029. The programme was officially launched on 19 June when an Indian defence delegation, led by Joint Secretary Dinesh Kumar, met with French officials, led by Lt Gen Gael Diaz De Tuesta, during the Paris Air Show. The Rafale was chosen over the Super Hornet due to commonality with the IAF’s Rafale fleet and ease of integrating Indian-origin systems. The aircraft will complement the existing Navy MiG-29K fleet and later the Indian-built Twin Engine Deck Based Fighter, operating on INS Vikramaditya and INS Vikrant. The deal was officially signed with France on 28 April 2025. During the 2010s, Poland sought 64 multirole combat aircraft from 2021 to replace its Su-22M4 and MiG-29s; in November 2017, the Armament Inspectorate launched the Harpia procurement process, with five entities—Saab, Lockheed Martin, Boeing, Leonardo, and Fights-On Logistics—expressing interest. On 28 May 2019, Poland formally requested 32 F-35As. Boeing first offered the Super Hornet to Switzerland in 2009, withdrawing in April 2008; the Swiss Air Force had previously considered the Gripen, which was blocked by voters in 2014. In March 2018, contenders for the Air 2030 program included Saab Gripen, Dassault Rafale, Eurofighter Typhoon, Boeing F/A-18E/F, and Lockheed Martin F-35, with a US$8 billion budget including ground-based air defence. In October 2018, Jane's reported Switzerland may limit purchases to single-engine fighters due to cost. The F/A-18E/F conducted demonstrations at Payerne Air Base in April 2019. On 30 June 2021, the Swiss Federal Council proposed buying 36 F-35As at up to CHF 6.035 billion (US$6.5 billion), citing cost and effectiveness; the anti-military group GSoA intended to contest the purchase in a national referendum, which gained 120,000 signatures by August 2022 (100,000 required). On 26 November 2021, Armasuisse agreed to purchase 36 F-35As; the deal was subject to parliamentary approval and the popular initiative. A parliamentary inquiry found the purchase worrisome but legal; the government proceeded without waiting for the initiative. On 15 September 2022, the Swiss National Council approved the purchase, signed on 19 September 2022, with deliveries starting in 2027 and ending by 2030. By 2018, Spain sought 68–72 fighters to replace its F/A-18A/B Hornets, with participants including Eurofighter Typhoon, Dassault Rafale, Boeing F/A-18E/F Advanced Super Hornet, and Lockheed F-35; on 22 June 2022, Spain ordered 20 Tranche 4 Typhoons to replace 20 ex-USN F/A-18s at the Canary Islands. The U.S. Marine Corps avoided the Super Hornet program due to concerns that it would come at the expense of F-35B STOVL fighters for amphibious ships; in 2011, the USMC agreed to equip five VMFA squadrons with F-35C to augment Navy carrier air wings. On 10 March 2009, Boeing offered the Super Hornet to Greece for its Next-Generation Fighter Program. On 1 August 2010, The Sunday Times reported the UK was considering cancelling F-35B orders and buying Super Hornets for its Queen Elizabeth-class carriers, claiming a £10 billion saving, citing ski-jump launch capability; ultimately, the UK chose a STOVL carrier with F-35Bs. The UAE was reported to have requested information on the Super Hornet in 2010. In early 2011, Bulgaria considered the F/A-18 as a MiG-21 replacement; after initially selecting the Gripen, the new government restarted the process, with the Super Hornet again under consideration, expected by July 2018; in December 2018, the Bulgarian Ministry of Defence selected 8 F-16V from the U.S. for approximately $1.05 billion as the preferred option. In 2012, Norway received an offer for at least one squadron of F/A-18s, noting its suitability for Northern Norwegian conditions. In 2014, Boeing partnered with Korean Airlines to offer the Advanced Super Hornet to the Republic of Korea Air Force as an alternative to the KF-X program, though downgrading would not provide South Korean industry with the same technological knowledge as developing a new fighter. Each U.S. Navy deployable "Fleet" VFA squadron has a standard unit establishment of 12 aircraft.
